literature.lead_zh: 本期马尔堡病毒研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 人单克隆抗体 MR191N 为非人灵长类动物提供完整的暴露后保护。先进的 RNA 靶向 siRNA、反义寡核苷酸和小分子核苷类似物(例如加利昔韦)在抑制病毒复制方面表现出强大的临床前功效。预防性平台,包括腺病毒载体 (ChAd3-MARV)、rVSV-MARV 和基于 mRNA 的 疫苗,正在通过早期临床和临床前评估取得进展。 [10.1080/14787210.2026.2723576]
暴发导致确诊病例608例,死亡102例,病死率为16.7%。此外,还有 34 名卫生工作者被感染,导致 5 人死亡。地理分布包括刚果民主共和国的伊图里省和乌干达坎帕拉的输入病例。 [10.18231/j.ijmmtd.63893.1788322901]
在两个研究组中,马尔堡病毒 的血清阳性率随着年龄的增长而增加,表明累积暴露。盖克杜实验室样本中还检测到了针对拉沙病毒等其他病原体的抗体。 [10.64898/2026.09.02.26362016]
literature.trend_or_risk_zh: 本期研究方向以入选文献实际覆盖的临床、流行病学、宿主生态、诊断或分子监测主题为准。
literature.lead_en: This reporting window highlights the following research developments.
key_findings_en: The human monoclonal antibody MR191N provides complete post-exposure protection in non-human primates. Advanced RNA-targeted siRNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, and small-molecule nucleoside analogues (e.g., galidesivir) demonstrate robust preclinical efficacy in suppressing viral replication. [10.1080/14787210.2026.2723576]

The outbreak resulted in 608 confirmed cases and 102 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 16.7%. Additionally, 34 health workers were infected, leading to five deaths. The geographic spread included the Ituri province in the DRC and imported cases in Kampala, Uganda. [10.18231/j.ijmmtd.63893.1788322901]

papers.title: Advances in therapeutics and vaccines for Marburg virus disease: challenges and future directions.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Marburg virus disease (MVD) is a highly lethal filovirus infection with case fatality rates of up to 88%. Although no virus-specific interventions have yet been approved, recent laboratory breakthroughs have markedly accelerated translational progress in vaccine and therapeutic development. AREAS COVERED: A hybrid methodological design was employed, combining macro-level bibliometric analysis with a targeted qualitative narrative review. As per the findings, the human monoclonal antibody MR191N provides complete post-exposure protection in non-human primates. Advanced RNA-targeted siRNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, and small-molecule nucleoside analogues (e.g. galidesivir) demonstrate robust preclinical efficacy in suppressing viral replication. Prophylactic platforms - including adenovirus-vectored (ChAd3-MARV), rVSV-MARV, and mRNA-based vaccines - are progressing through early-phase clinical and preclinical evaluation. Bibliometric analysis, however, reveals pronounced geographic disparities: high-income nations dominate scientific output (United States: 31.7%), while endemic African countries remain severely underrepresented in global collaboration networks. EXPERT OPINION: Addressing MVD requires a coordinated transition from experimental research to licensed, field-ready interventions. This necessitates adaptive trial designs, expanded diagnostic models, and synergistic combination therapies. Ultimately, correcting global research inequities and embedding robust, cross-border One Health surveillance infrastructure are essential to transforming scientific advances into equitable, rapid-response solutions for endemic regions.

For reprints contact: reprint@ipinnovative.com The 2026 public health emergency involving the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) across the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda has exposed significant vulnerabilities in global health preparedness. As of June 8, 2026, the outbreak has resulted in 608 confirmed cases and 102 deaths, representing a case fatality rate of 16.7%. The geographic spread has reached the Ituri province in the DRC, including the health zones of Bunia, Mongbwalu, and Rwampara, while imported cases have been identified as far as Kampala, Uganda. A particularly concerning aspect of this emergency is its impact on the healthcare workforce, with 34 confirmed infections and five deaths among health workers.1,2 An extensive review of literature for 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) emergency in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, highlights the critical need for species-specific medical countermeasures. As initial diagnostic tests failed to identify the virus due to target mismatch, experts advocate for broad molecular screening and genomic sequencing to ensure rapid detection. Preclinical research evaluates various vaccines and therapies, noting that while recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus platforms show promise in animals, no licensed treatments exist specifically for BVD so far. The Africa CDC has issued guidelines to enhance border surveillance and infection control while cautioning against general travel bans that could harm regional security. Furthermore, long-term studies on Ebola survivors reveal the complexity of viral persistence in bodily reservoirs and the necessity of longitudinal clinical follow-up. Collectively, these documents emphasise that regional coordination and tailored research are essential for managing this distinct and neglected ebolavirus.1,2 1. Diagnostic Challenges and Genomic Divergence A primary obstacle in managing this outbreak is the “diagnostic target mismatch”. Because BDBV differs by more than 30% at the genomic level from other ebolaviruses, standard molecular tests optimised for the Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV) often fail to detect it. During the initial stages of the 2026 outbreak, standard RT-qPCR testing using “Ebola Xpert” cartridges returned negative results. Accurate identification was achieved only after the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB) employed broader genomic sequencing and metagenomic analysis.3 To address these vulnerabilities, a multi-tiered diagnostic workflow is essential. This includes: The Recommended Diagnostic Workflow for BDBV: 1. Initial screening for all filoviruses using broad RT-PCR, this is essential when species identity is unknown. 2. Sanger sequencing and assigning species level identity based on the sequence of amplicons identified from broad RT-PCR. 3. Agnostic detection based on metagenomics for unknown or critically divergent isolates. 4. Confirmation through species-specific qRT-PCR after the target species is identified. 2. Public Health and Regulatory Response The Africa CDC has spearheaded the response, implementing guidelines focused on enhanced surveillance and tightened screening at borders, airports, and seaports. These measures utilize integrated reporting systems that combine paper-based and electronic platforms to track key performance indicators. Crucially, health authorities have adopted a risk-based approach, avoiding blanket travel bans that could undermine national security and regional trade.4 3. The Evolving Landscape of Medical Countermeasures Currently, no licensed vaccines or therapeutics are specifically approved for BDBV. However, several candidates are being fast-tracked through preclinical and clinical evaluation.1,2,5 3.1. Obeldesivir, an oral candidate, is being prioritized by the WHO for post-exposure prophylaxis. Monoclonal antibody cocktails, such as MBP134AF and BDBV289-N, have demonstrated high levels of protection in non-human primate models (Table 1 below). While the EBOV treatment, Maftivimab (Inmazeb), shows neutralisation in laboratory settings, it lacks robust in vivo efficacy data for BDBV.5,6 Table 1. MBP134AF NHP/Ferret High therapeutic protection in both models. Remdesivir In Vitro Confirmed B DBV polymerase susceptibility. rVSV∆G /BDBV-GP NHP PEP 5/6 survived when treated ~20 mins post-exposure. 3.2. Vaccines Three specific candidates are currently considered trial-ready: a monovalent rVSV-based vaccine from IAVI, a ChAdOx1-based candidate from the University of Oxford/Serum Institute of India, and an mRNA-based platform from Moderna. Notably, the licensed ERVEBO vaccine for EBOV does not provide confirmed cross-protection against BDBV.5,7 4. Viral Persistence and the Threat of Re-emergence Lessons from EBOV survivors indicate that viral clearance from the blood does not necessarily mean the virus has been eliminated from the body. The virus can hide in “immune privileged niches” (IPNs), such as the testes, brain, eyes, and mammary glands. Persistence in the testes remains a critical risk for human-to-human transmission through seminal fluid. Meta-analysis shows that while viral carriage drops over time, approximately 50% of survivors may still harbour the virus after 12 months, and nearly 10% may remain positive for up to five years. Persistence in other sites can lead to severe complications, including sight-threatening uveitis or fatal meningoencephalitis months after recovery. Viral RNA has also been detected in breast milk up to 500 days post-discharge, raising risks for vertical transmission. Molecular research suggests three theories for this persistence: minor polymerase mutations leading to low-rate replication, defective interfering genomes that suppress viral load, or a lack of immune pressure within specific niches.8 5. Implementation and Strategic Priorities Moving forward, the WHO Filovirus Research and Development Roadmap emphasises the need for pre-positioned infrastructure and regional leadership. Priorities include: 1. Regional Leadership: Outbreak control and clinical trials must be led by African institutions like the Africa CDC and the African Medicines Agency (AMA). 2. Trial Readiness: Standardised protocols must be ready to evaluate medical countermeasures during the brief windows of active outbreaks. 3. Comprehensive Survivor Care: Longitudinal follow-up is necessary to manage “post-Ebola sequelae” (such as fatigue and arthralgia) and to monitor for potential viral flare-ups. 4. Ring Vaccination: This strategy should be employed around survivors to mitigate the risk of sexual transmission and prevent new outbreak clusters.4,8 In summary, the 2026 BDBV emergency highlights that managing this neglected ebolavirus requires species-specific diagnostics, tailored research, and a robust, regionally led public health framework. 6. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges posed by the 2026 Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) outbreak, highlighting the need for species-specific medical countermeasures due to the virus's distinct genomic characteristics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a review of literature and public health data from the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, focusing on the impact on healthcare workers and the geographic spread of the virus.
analysis.methods: Diagnostic challenges were addressed through broad molecular screening and genomic sequencing, with specific mention of using Sanger sequencing to identify species-level identity based on amplicon sequences from broad RT-PCR.
analysis.main_results: The outbreak resulted in 608 confirmed cases and 102 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 16.7%. Additionally, 34 health workers were infected, leading to five deaths. The geographic spread included the Ituri province in the DRC and imported cases in Kampala, Uganda.

papers.title: Seroprevalence of viral hemorrhagic fevers and arboviral infections among febrile patients in Forest Guinea
papers.abstract: Between 2017 and 2024, routine diagnostics surveillance in Guinea detected several confirmed viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF) cases among febrile patients. To assess exposure to Lassa virus and other viral pathogens, we conducted a retrospective cross-sectional seroprevalence study in Forest Guinea (Guéckédou and N′Zérékoré). Lassa virus seroprevalence was 56.0% in the Guéckédou study group and 29.8% in the N′Zérékoré study group. Seropositivity increased with age in both study groups, suggesting cumulative exposure. Samples from Guéckédou laboratory were also tested for other pathogens, and antibodies against Marburg virus (5.8%), Zika virus (5.4%) and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (1.2%) were detected.
